Lucayan

Also find this entry through: Lucayans

Lucayan is a historical reading label for Indigenous communities of the Bahamian archipelago, including the Bahamas and Turks and Caicos. Museum interpretation and ceramic research introduce island settlement, skilled material production and exchange without determining anyone’s present ancestry or identity.

Read the sources [1] Turks and Caicos National Museum [3] William F. Keegan, Lindsay C. Bloch, Emily C. Kracht and Michael P. Pateman; Journal of Caribbean Archaeology 22

01

A historical regional label

The Turks and Caicos museum relates the Lucayan label to wider Taíno histories and discusses alternative settlement interpretations. Its account of Spanish enslavement provides colonial context. Its outdated disappearance and technological-ranking language is not adopted; a historical name is not a verdict on living descendants.

Read the sources [1] Turks and Caicos National Museum

02

Making pottery on limestone islands

Florida Museum researchers describe red Palmetto Ware with burned conch-shell inclusions and investigate how potters worked with limited local clay. Their experiments help explain material choices; they do not recreate an individual historical potter’s own explanation.

Read the sources [2] Florida Museum of Natural History

03

Exchange and the limits of archaeological samples

The 2022 pottery study distinguishes locally made vessels from imports associated with the Greater Antilles. Its authors caution that differences between household floors, refuse deposits and periods affect comparisons. Their exchange model is a research interpretation built from incomplete samples.

Read the sources [3] William F. Keegan, Lindsay C. Bloch, Emily C. Kracht and Michael P. Pateman; Journal of Caribbean Archaeology 22

04

Reading fuelwood evidence with its limits

Berman, Pearsall and Ritzheimer compare charred wood from four sites on San Salvador and Grand Bahama. They interpret collection as a mixture of nearby availability and purposeful selection, while noting that preservation and sample context affect what survives. This is evidence from selected archaeological assemblages, not a description of every Lucayan household or today’s forests.

Read the sources [4] Mary Jane Berman,Deborah M. Pearsall and Caleb Ritzheimer; Vegetation History and Archaeobotany / Springer Nature
